pages.name: 拼音
pages.sub: Letters that don't sound like English

blocks.text: Pinyin spells Mandarin with the Latin alphabet. You'll see it on maps, in station names and in every dictionary app, and it's the easiest way to read how a word is said.

Every syllable has a starting sound (b, sh, zh…), the rest of the syllable (a, ian, ong…) and a tone, shown by the mark over a vowel. Most letters sound roughly as in English. These are the ones that don't. Tap one to hear the example.
Letters to relearn

blocks.text: Puff or no puff
b, d and g are not voiced as in English. They're like the p, t and k in "spy", "sty" and "sky", with no puff of air. p, t and k have a strong puff.

blocks.desc: rougher than English h, a little like "ch" in Scottish "loch"

blocks.text: In Taiwan
Many people in Taiwan say zh, ch and sh much like z, c and s, so 是 shì can sound like sì. Endings -in and -ing, and -en and -eng, can also sound alike. Either way you'll be understood.
Mandarin is tonal: the pitch of a syllable is part of the word. mā, má, mǎ and mà are four different words. Pinyin shows the tone with a mark over a vowel.

blocks.label: ā · 1st tone
blocks.desc: high and level, like holding a note

blocks.label: a · neutral tone
blocks.desc: short and light, with no mark

blocks.text: 媽 is mother, 麻 is numb, 馬 is horse and 罵 is to scold. In everyday speech the 3rd tone usually stays low and only rises when you stop on it.
Tones that change in speech
Pinyin usually writes each syllable's own tone, but three common changes happen as you speak. Knowing them makes phrases sound right.
Taiwan's tones

Taiwanese Mandarin uses the light neutral tone less often than the Mandarin of Beijing, so you'll hear full tones where some textbooks write a neutral one. This app's readings follow Taiwan's dictionaries.
A handful of phrases covers most polite moments. 不好意思 is the one you'll use most in Taiwan: excuse me, sorry to bother you, and a small sorry, all in one.
These phrases keep a conversation going when you're lost. People in Taiwan are usually patient and happy to help a visitor who tries a little Mandarin.
Chinese numbers are regular. Learn zero to ten and you can build every number up to 99.
Building bigger numbers

11 is "ten one", 20 is "two ten" and 35 is "three ten five". After that come 百 bǎi (hundred), 千 qiān (thousand) and 萬 wàn (ten thousand). Chinese counts large numbers in ten-thousands, so 50,000 is 五萬, "five ten-thousands".
Two: 二 or 兩?
Use 二 èr when counting, in phone numbers and inside numbers like 十二 (12). Use 兩 liǎng for "two of something" and, usually, before 百, 千 and 萬.
Zero in the middle
A gap inside a number is read as 零: 105 is "one hundred zero five". Phone numbers are read digit by digit.
Taiwan's money is the New Taiwan dollar (NT$). Price tags say 元 yuán, but in speech people say 塊 kuài: 五十塊 is NT$50. Coins are 1, 5, 10 and 50; the common notes are 100, 500 and 1,000.

pages.name: 句子
pages.sub: Six patterns that go a long way

blocks.text: Chinese has no verb endings, plurals or articles: words never change form. Word order and a few small words do the work.
1. Who, does, what
The order is the same as in English: subject, verb, object.
2. 是 shì joins nouns, 很 hěn comes before adjectives
是 means "is" between two nouns. Before an adjective, use 很 hěn instead. Here it barely means "very".
3. Yes-or-no questions with 嗎 ma
Add 嗎 to the end of a statement to turn it into a question. To answer, repeat the verb: 有 (yes, there is) or 沒有 (no).
4. Saying no: 不 bù and 沒 méi
不 makes most verbs and adjectives negative. 有 (to have, there is) takes 沒 instead.
5. Question words stay put
To ask where, put 哪裡 nǎlǐ where the answer would go: "bathroom is where?". 什麼 shénme (what) and 多少 duōshǎo (how much) work the same way.
6. Counting things with 個 gè
Between a number and a noun goes a measure word. There are many, but 個 works for most things when you're not sure.
In many small restaurants you order at the counter or tick a paper menu, and pay first or on the way out. Tipping isn't expected anywhere in Taiwan.
在 zài means "is at". Put the place first and 在哪裡 after it to ask where something is.
Times go from big to small: day first, then the hour. 點 diǎn is o'clock and 半 bàn is half past.
Days of the week
星期 xīngqí is "week". Monday to Saturday are numbered: 星期一 is day one. Sunday is 星期天. You'll also hear 禮拜 lǐbài used the same way.

Zhuyin (注音符號) is Taiwan's own way of writing the sounds of Mandarin. It's also called bopomofo, after its first four symbols ㄅㄆㄇㄈ. Children in Taiwan learn it before characters, and it appears beside characters in children's books and dictionaries.
Why you might want it
It's how Taiwan types. Most people here use zhuyin keyboards on their phones, so you'll see it on screens around you.
It describes Mandarin sounds directly, with no English spelling habits to unlearn: no q that sounds like ch.
Many learning materials in Taiwan use it, so it helps if you plan to study here.
Why you might not need it
Pinyin is enough to read pronunciations, look words up and type Chinese on your phone with a pinyin keyboard.
Street signs, maps and the MRT use the Latin alphabet, sometimes with older spellings such as Taipei for Táiběi.
Learning 37 new symbols takes a few weeks of practice. On a short trip, phrases are a better use of your time.
How it works

Each symbol is one sound. A syllable has up to three symbols: a starting sound, a middle ㄧ, ㄨ or ㄩ, and an ending. Beside characters they're written top to bottom. Tone marks follow the syllable: the 1st tone has no mark, and the neutral tone's dot ˙ goes in front.

blocks.text: 7-Eleven, FamilyMart (全家), Hi-Life (萊爾富) and OK Mart are everywhere and open around the clock. You can pay, top up transit cards, print and pick up parcels there. The clerk asks the same few questions every time, and 要 (yes) or 不用 (no need) answers most of them.

In many small restaurants you tick dishes on a paper order sheet and hand it in at the counter. Night market stalls are often cash only. Tipping isn't expected.

At drink stands (手搖飲) you choose the size, sugar and ice. Sugar goes from 全糖 (full) through 少糖, 半糖 and 微糖 to 無糖 (none). Ice goes from 正常冰 (regular) through 少冰 and 微冰 to 去冰 (no ice), or 熱的 for hot.

An EasyCard (悠遊卡) or iPASS (一卡通) pays for the MRT, buses, YouBike and convenience stores. Don't eat or drink inside MRT stations or trains: the fines are real. Taxi drivers rarely speak English, so show them the address in Chinese.

Public bathrooms are free and easy to find in MRT stations, parks, department stores and many convenience stores. It's worth carrying tissues: not every bathroom has paper.

pages.name: 口語
pages.sub: Slang, Taiwanese words, what not to say

blocks.text: Textbook Mandarin is polite but a bit stiff. These are the short words people in Taiwan actually use with friends, at markets and at work. Most are friendly and safe; the last group is for recognising, not saying.
Many come from Taiwanese (台語), Taiwan's other everyday language. People usually smile when a visitor uses one.
Everyday reactions
From Taiwanese
You'll hear
Recognise, don't say
You'll hear these among friends, in traffic and on TV. Knowing them helps; saying them as a visitor can go badly wrong.

phrases.note: Two 3rd tones in a row: the first becomes a 2nd tone, so it's said ní hǎo.
不 bù becomes bú before a 4th tone: bú yào.
一 yī becomes yí before a 4th tone and yì before the other tones: yí gè.
